Matthew 1:1 and Luke 3:31 trace Jesus as the son of David.
After AD 70 the temple was never rebuilt; an attempt under Emperor Julian in AD 363 failed (Ammianus Marcellinus, History 23.1.2-3).

Dispensationalists agree Christ sits on his Father's throne now (Revelation 3:21), but hold that David's throne will be set up on earth in Jerusalem during the millennium, with a restored temple described in Ezekiel 40-48.
What did God remove when he shook "not only the earth but also heaven" (Hebrews 12:26-27)?
On the fulfilled reading, he removed the shakable old-covenant order: temple, priesthood and animal sacrifice. The unshakable kingdom remained.

Hebrews quotes Haggai 2:6: God will once more shake earth and heaven. The writer explains that this means removing things that can be shaken, "as of things that are made," so that what cannot be shaken remains (Hebrews 12:26-27). He then says believers are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). The letter has already said the old covenant is "ready to vanish away" (Hebrews 8:13). On this reading, the shaking came in AD 70. The temple fell, the priesthood stopped, and the sacrifices ended. Those things were "made with hands" and temporary. What stayed was Christ's kingdom and his spiritual temple.
Hebrews 8:13, written before AD 70, says the old covenant is "growing old" and near to disappearing.
Daily sacrifice in the temple stopped in July/August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2.1).

Many interpreters read the shaking as the final judgment at the end of history, when the physical creation is renewed. Others see a partial fulfillment at Christ's first coming and a final one at his return.
If the stone temple was thrown down, what temple did God build in its place?
A temple of people. Jews and Gentiles joined in Christ are built into a spiritual house with Christ as the cornerstone.

Peter calls believers "living stones" being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood that offers spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5). Paul says Gentiles who were far off have been brought near by Christ's blood (Ephesians 2:13). Jews and Gentiles together are no longer strangers but fellow citizens and members of God's household. They are built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone, growing into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:19-21). On this reading, the gathering of the elect in Matthew 24:31 is the building of this new temple out of all nations. The message is no longer only for "the lost sheep of Israel" (Matthew 15:24) but for the scattered children of God (John 11:52).
1 Corinthians 3:16: "you are God's temple."
Acts 15:14-17: James applies Amos's rebuilt "tent of David" to Gentiles coming in.

All Christian views see the church as God's temple now. Dispensationalists add that a literal temple will also be built in Jerusalem in the future, either for the Antichrist's period or for the millennium.
Does Matthew 24:31 mean angels will carry Jewish people from around the world back to Jerusalem?
This reading says no. Old Testament "gathering" texts never use angels, and the gathering is the gospel bringing people into Christ.

Some dispensational writers teach that angels will supernaturally bring scattered Israelites back to the land at Christ's return. One writer joked that it will be angels "rather than El Al airline." God can do anything (Mark 10:27). Yet the question is what Jesus meant. When Moses and Isaiah speak of God gathering his people from the ends of the earth, no angels appear (Deuteronomy 30:1-4; Isaiah 11:12). God gathers through repentance, return and his own hand. On this reading, Matthew 24:31 describes the worldwide mission that followed the fall of the old order: messengers sent out with the gospel to gather the chosen from every nation.
Deuteronomy 30:3-4: God himself gathers his people "from the farthest parts under heaven."
Isaiah 11:12: God raises a banner for the nations to gather the dispersed.

Dispensationalists, such as J. Dwight Pentecost, see a literal final regathering of Israel by angels after the tribulation. Other futurists see the gathering of all believers at the resurrection (compare Matthew 13:41, 49, where angels gather at the end).
Can the "angels" of Matthew 24:31 be human messengers?
Yes. The Greek word angelos means messenger, and Scripture uses it for prophets, priests, John the Baptist and others.

Angelos is the ordinary Greek word for a messenger. Context tells whether a heavenly or a human messenger is meant. Haggai is called "the Lord's messenger" (Haggai 1:13). The priest is the messenger of the Lord of hosts (Malachi 2:7). John the Baptist is the messenger sent ahead (Matthew 11:10). Jesus sent messengers ahead of him into a Samaritan village (Luke 9:52). Rahab received the "messengers" Joshua sent (James 2:25). Even a dispensational writer such as Ed Hindson notes that the "angels" of the seven churches may be their leaders (Revelation 2:1). On this reading, the angels of Matthew 24:31 are gospel preachers sent out to gather God's people.
2 Chronicles 36:15-16: God sent his messengers again and again, but the people mocked them until there was no remedy. This pattern led to Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC.
Mark 1:2 quotes Malachi 3:1 about John: "I send my messenger before your face."

Most commentators take "angels" in Matthew 24:31 as heavenly beings, because elsewhere the Son of Man comes "with his angels" (Matthew 16:27; 25:31) and angels reap at the end of the age (Matthew 13:39).
What do "the four winds" and "from one end of heaven to the other" mean?
They mean everywhere. The gathering reaches the whole world, not only the land of Israel.

"Four winds" is a common Bible picture for the four directions (Zechariah 2:6; Daniel 7:2; Revelation 7:1). "From one end of heaven to the other" means the whole horizon (Deuteronomy 4:32). Mark's parallel adds "from the end of the earth to the end of heaven" (Mark 13:27). On this reading, Jesus is saying that his people will be gathered from all over the world. The mission that began among "the lost sheep of Israel" (Matthew 15:24) now reaches the nations, as he promised: many will come from east and west to eat with Abraham (Matthew 8:11). The same language was used of judgment on Elam, scattered to the four winds (Jeremiah 49:36).
Acts begins in Jerusalem and ends in Rome. To a Jew in Jerusalem, Rome was "the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8).
Revelation 7:9: a great crowd from every nation, tribe, people and language.

Futurists read the same phrases as the worldwide gathering at Christ's visible return. Both sides agree the words mean "everywhere"; they differ on whether the gathering is the gospel mission or a single final event.
Does Bible language like "four corners of the earth" teach a flat or square earth?
No. It is a figure of speech for the whole world, just as "the four winds" means every direction.

Scripture speaks of the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:12; Revelation 7:1). It also pictures the earth as a house with foundations and pillars, and heaven as a house with many rooms (John 14:2). These are images, not science. Isaiah also speaks of God sitting above "the circle of the earth" (Isaiah 40:22). The point of such language is God's rule over the whole world. This matters for prophecy too. If we do not read "four corners" with wooden literalism, we should not demand wooden literalism for clouds, falling stars and angel trumpets. Each image must be read the way Scripture uses it.
People still say "the sun rises" without teaching that the sun moves round the earth.
Ezekiel 7:2 announces an end on "the four corners of the land" of Israel.

All major Christian views accept that "four corners" is figurative. The debate is over which details in prophecy are figurative and which are literal; futurists hold that historical narrative and plain prediction should be taken literally unless the text signals otherwise.
What is the "great trumpet" in Matthew 24:31?
On this reading, it is the gospel call. It echoes the silver trumpets that gathered Israel and the Jubilee trumpet that proclaimed release.

In Numbers 10:1-10 God told Moses to make two silver trumpets to call the assembly and to start the camp marching. The Jubilee year was announced by trumpet on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 25:9-10). It meant release of slaves and return of land. Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah 61, the "acceptable year of the Lord," and said it was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16-21). Isaiah 27:13 says a great trumpet will sound and the scattered will come to worship. Prophets were told to lift their voice like a trumpet (Isaiah 58:1). On this reading, the great trumpet is the proclamation of the gospel calling people from every nation into God's assembly.
Isaiah 27:13: "the great trumpet shall be blown," and the lost in Assyria and Egypt come to worship.
2 Corinthians 6:2: "now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation."

Futurists link this trumpet to the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52 and the trumpet of 1 Thessalonians 4:16, and so to a single final event. Pretribulationists usually separate the Matthew 24 trumpet (for Israel) from the rapture trumpet (for the church).
What does the word "gather together" in Matthew 24:31 suggest?
The verb is episynago, related to synagoge. God is gathering a new assembly in Christ, made of believing Jews and Gentiles.

Matthew 24:31 uses the verb episynago, "gather together." It is related to synagoge, a gathering or synagogue. Jesus used the same verb when he wept over Jerusalem: he longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks, but they were not willing (Matthew 23:37). On this reading, after the judgment on the city he gathers his elect from all over the world into a new assembly. John says Jesus died to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:52). Peter tells such people that once they were not a people, but now they are God's people (1 Peter 2:9-10). Note that the gathered church began with Jewish believers. Many thousands of Jews believed in Jerusalem itself (Acts 21:20).
Matthew 23:37 and 24:31 use the same verb, linking the lament and the gathering.
Hebrews 10:25 uses the related noun for believers meeting together.
Many futurists note that Paul uses the noun form for "our gathering together to him" at Christ's coming (2 Thessalonians 2:1), and take Matthew 24:31 as the same future event.
Why does this reading link the worldwide gathering of the elect with the time after AD 70?
The gospel went to the Jew first. After the old order fell, the mission to all nations went forward without the temple at its centre.

The gospel began at Pentecost, but it went first to Jews (Romans 1:16). Paul usually began in the synagogue (Acts 17:1-2). The Jerusalem church kept close ties to the temple (Acts 21:26). When the temple fell, the old centre was gone. On this reading, the mission to the nations went forward in new fullness, as Christ had commanded: make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18-20). The commentator R. V. G. Tasker argued that only after the old order ended could the church, now clearly distinct from the temple system, sound the gospel trumpet across the world. History shows the elect still being gathered from every tribe and language.
The early Christian movement spread widely across the Roman world in the second and third centuries, even under persecution.
Romans 15:19-24 shows Paul planning a mission as far as Spain.
Other views point out that the Gentile mission was already strong well before AD 70 (Acts 13-28; Colossians 1:6). Futurists see Matthew 24:31 as the end of the mission, not its continuation.
Does the fig tree budding in Matthew 24:32-33 point to Israel becoming a state in 1948?
This reading says no. The fig tree is a simple picture from nature: when leaves appear, summer is near. The "things" were the signs before AD 70.

Hal Lindsey called Israel's rebirth on 14 May 1948 the most important sign, and he read the fig tree as Israel. If a generation is about forty years, he suggested, all these things could happen within about forty years of 1948. Chuck Smith said the generation alive in 1948 would not pass away before Christ came. On this reading, the whole scheme rests on one assumption: that the fig tree means the modern state. But Jesus explains his own picture. When the branch is tender and leaves come out, you know summer is near; so when you see "all these things," know that he is near (Matthew 24:32-33). "All these things" are the signs he has just listed. Those signs were for his hearers, and they came before AD 70.
Lindsey, The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), linked 1948 + about 40 years with the end.
In 1988 and the years after, many readers who had expected Christ by then had to rethink.

Many dispensationalists still see 1948 as a key sign of the last days, even if they no longer use a forty-year count. Others in the same tradition, like John Walvoord, did not read the fig tree as Israel but still expected a future tribulation.
Is the fig tree ever used in Scripture as a symbol of national Israel?
Figs and fig trees do picture Israel's condition in some texts, but not its future restoration. In the Gospels the barren fig tree pictures judgment.

John Walvoord argued that the fig tree is not clearly used as a symbol of Israel. Good and bad figs picture exiles and those left behind (Jeremiah 24:1-8). Hosea compares Israel's fathers to early figs (Hosea 9:10). In Judges 9:10-11 the fig tree in Jotham's story is not Israel. In the Gospels, Jesus curses a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and it withers (Matthew 21:18-20; Mark 11:12-14, 20-21). This happened in the week he judged the temple. On this reading, if the fig tree links with Israel at all, it stands for a fruitless system facing judgment, not a nation about to bloom again. Even so, Matthew 24:32 does not draw on that link; it uses the tree as a seasonal clock.
Luke 13:6-9: a fig tree with no fruit for three years is given one more year before being cut down.
Mark 11 sandwiches the cursing of the fig tree around the cleansing of the temple.

Some futurists say the cursed fig tree pictures Israel set aside, and the budding fig tree pictures Israel restored. Others accept Walvoord's view that the tree is only a natural illustration and does not stand for Israel.
What does Luke's wording, "the fig tree and all the trees," add to the parable?
It shows the point is ordinary seasons, not one nation. Any tree in leaf tells you summer is near.

Luke records Jesus saying: look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they put out leaves, you know summer is near. So when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near (Luke 21:29-31). If the fig tree were a code for Israel, what would "all the trees" stand for? On this reading, the added words show that Jesus was using a common sight from nature. Leaves on trees signal a coming season. In the same way, the signs he listed would signal that the judgment and the kingdom's coming in power were at the door. Near to what? Near to fulfilling his promise about the temple within that generation.
In Israel, fig leaves appear in late spring, shortly before summer fruit.
Song of Songs 2:11-13 uses the fig tree's early fruit as a simple sign that spring has come.

Some futurists answer that "all the trees" may represent other nations reviving in the end times alongside Israel. Most commentators of all schools agree the illustration is mainly seasonal, though they differ on whether "these things" point to AD 70, to a future tribulation, or to both.
Does the fig tree picture allow a forty-year "generation of the fig tree"?
This reading says no. Leaves in spring point to one coming summer. A single season is in view, not decades of waiting.

Some teachers speak of "the generation of the fig tree," meaning the generation born after 1948. On this reading, that misuses the picture. Leaves are a short-term sign. When you see them, summer is weeks away, not forty or fifty summers. In the same way, when Jesus' hearers saw the listed signs, the judgment was close. The leaves in the parable correspond to the signs of the 60s AD: false messiahs, war, armies around Jerusalem. They have nothing to do with 1948, the Six-Day War of 1967, or the peace accords of 1993. Each of those events has been offered as "the" sign, and each forecast built on them has failed.
Jerusalem was surrounded by Roman armies first under Cestius Gallus in AD 66 and then under Titus in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19.4-7; 5.2.1-3).
The Oslo Accords were signed in 1993; some prophecy writers presented them as the start of the seven-year tribulation.

Futurists who use the "fig tree generation" idea answer that the signs begin with Israel's rebirth and then build over a lifetime. Many futurist scholars now reject fixed-length generation counts, while still seeing modern Israel as prophetically significant.
If Israel's rebirth were the chief sign, why would Jesus hide it in an unexplained picture?
This reading argues he would not. Jesus spoke clearly about non-signs and gave a clear sign: the abomination and armies around Jerusalem.

In Matthew 24:4-14 Jesus spent many words warning what should not be taken as signs of the end: wars, rumours of wars, famines and earthquakes are only the beginning. Then he gave a definite sign: when you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, flee (Matthew 24:15). Luke explains it as Jerusalem surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). On this reading, it would be strange for Jesus, after such clarity, to make the most important sign of all a symbol he never defined. The fig tree comes after the main teaching, as a summary picture of timing. It does not introduce a new, hidden sign.
Matthew 24:6: "see that you are not troubled... the end is not yet."
Luke 21:20 names the sign plainly: armies surrounding Jerusalem.
Futurists respond that prophecy is often understood fully only when fulfilled (Daniel 12:4, 9), so the fig tree's meaning could become clear later, as they believe it did in 1948.
What pictures does the New Testament use for God's people, if not the fig tree?
The vine, the olive tree, the lump of dough and the flock. These describe one people of God joined to Christ.

Jesus calls himself the true vine and his disciples the branches (John 15:1-8). Paul pictures one olive tree, with natural branches broken off by unbelief and wild branches grafted in by faith. Natural branches can be grafted back in if they believe (Romans 11:16-24). He speaks of the first part of the dough making the whole lump holy (Romans 11:16). Jesus calls his people a little flock (Luke 12:32) and says he has other sheep to bring in, so there will be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). On this reading, these pictures stress one people in Christ, not a separate future program for a political state.
Isaiah 5:1-7 already pictured Israel as God's vineyard; Jesus applies the vine picture to himself.
John 10:16: other sheep, one flock, one shepherd.

Dispensationalists and many others note that Romans 11 itself speaks of a future turning of Israel ("all Israel will be saved," Romans 11:26). They say the olive tree shows a distinct future for ethnic Israel within God's plan.
Why is Matthew 24:34 called the key to the whole chapter?
Because it sets the time limit. Jesus said all the things he had just described would happen before his hearers' generation passed away.

Jesus said: truly, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place (Matthew 24:34). The verse looks back over everything from verse 4 to verse 33. J. Marcellus Kik called it the key to Matthew 24. On the fulfilled reading, once this time marker is taken at face value, the rest of the chapter falls into place. The temple's fall, the tribulation, the cosmic language and the Son of Man's coming all belong to the first century. Without this key, every generation can find its own news in the chapter, and wild speculation follows. With it, the chapter becomes a fulfilled prophecy that confirms Jesus as a true prophet.
Matthew 23:36 uses the same phrase: "all these things will come upon this generation." Few doubt that meant his hearers.
Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32 repeat the time limit in nearly the same words.

Futurists answer that "this generation" means the generation alive when the signs begin, or that "all these things" refers only to verses 4-28. Some scholars think Jesus expected the end in his generation and was mistaken, a view all the views in this study reject.
How does Luke 21:36 help decide who "this generation" is?
Jesus told the same listeners to pray that they might escape the things "about to" happen. "You" and "this generation" are the same people.

In Luke's account Jesus says: stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are about to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man (Luke 21:36). The "you" are the disciples he was speaking to. They were to watch and pray. The events were "about to" take place. On this reading, the meaning of "you" settles the meaning of "this generation." Jesus was not addressing unknown people two thousand years later while speaking to Peter, James, John and Andrew (Mark 13:3). The warnings were personal and urgent: flee, pray, watch. They make sense only if the hearers would live through the events.
Mark 13:3 names the four disciples who asked the question privately.
Luke 21:20: "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is near."

Futurists reply that "you" can mean the disciples as representatives of all believers, including those living at the end. Jesus often addresses the church through the apostles (Matthew 28:20). So, they say, the warnings to watch and pray apply to every later generation of believers too.
Can the Greek word genea in Matthew 24:34 mean "race" rather than "generation"?
Standard lexicons place Matthew 24:34 under "generation," that is, people living at the same time. "Race" is a rare meaning that does not fit here.

Some writers, including Arno Gaebelein and the Scofield Reference Bible, said genea here means "race": the Jewish people will not die out before the end. But the main Greek lexicons do not support this for Matthew 24:34. Thayer defines genea as the whole multitude of people living at the same time and lists Matthew 24:34 and Mark 13:30 under that sense. The Bauer-Arndt-Gingrich lexicon notes the "nation" view but places Matthew 24:34 under "contemporaries." Kittel's Theological Dictionary says this generation is to be understood in a time sense. On this reading, the natural, unforced meaning is the generation then alive.
Thayer, Greek-English Lexicon (1889): genea = "the whole multitude of men living at the same time," citing Matthew 24:34.
Matthew 1:17 uses genea for the fourteen generations from Abraham to David.

Some scholars, including William Hendriksen, argued genea can mean a kind of people or a race marked by unbelief, so Jesus meant the Jewish people, or unbelieving humanity, would last until the end. Others read "this kind of generation."
What is the difference between genea and genos?
Genos is the usual word for race or nation. Genea is the usual word for generation. The Gospel writers used genea in this verse.

When the New Testament wants to say "race," "nation" or "stock," it normally uses genos. Paul calls himself "of the stock (genos) of Israel" (Philippians 3:5). Peter calls the church "a chosen race (genos)" (1 Peter 2:9). Barnabas is a Levite "of Cyprus by birth (genos)" (Acts 4:36). Gaebelein cited 1 Peter 2:9 for his "race" view, but that verse uses genos, not genea. On this reading, if Matthew, Mark and Luke had meant "this race," they had a clear word for it. All three chose genea instead. That choice supports the ordinary meaning: the people living in that period.
Mark 7:26: the woman was a Syrophoenician "by race" (genos).
Acts 7:19: Pharaoh dealt craftily with "our race" (genos).

Those who favour "race" say the two words overlap in some Greek writers and that genea can carry the idea of a family line. They argue the theological sense, an unbelieving kind of people, fits Jesus' usage.
How does Matthew use "this generation" elsewhere in his Gospel?
Every time, it refers to Jesus' own contemporaries, often to warn them of judgment.

Matthew uses "this generation" in several places. Jesus compares this generation to children in the market who will not dance or mourn (Matthew 11:16). He calls them an evil and adulterous generation seeking a sign (Matthew 12:39; 16:4). The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation (Matthew 12:41-42). He says, "O faithless generation, how long shall I be with you?" (Matthew 17:17). He warns that the blood of the prophets will come on this generation (Matthew 23:36). In every case the people are those Jesus faced. On this reading, a sound method compares Matthew with Matthew. A writer such as William Hendriksen, who argued for another meaning, did not let these uses decide the case.
Matthew 23:36 comes just a few verses before 24:34 and uses the same phrase for the same people.
Matthew 12:45: "so shall it be also unto this wicked generation."
Some answer that these texts use "generation" in a moral sense ("evil generation"), so it describes a kind of people, not a time period. The moral sense, they say, could extend to later unbelievers.
Does "save yourselves from this crooked generation" (Acts 2:40) show that genea means the Jewish race?
No. Peter, himself a Jew, was not calling his own race crooked. He meant the generation of that time, which faced judgment.

Some point to Acts 2:40 to support "race." Peter urges his listeners: be saved from this crooked generation. But Peter was Jewish. He stayed Jewish after he followed Christ. The three thousand who believed that day were Jews and converts to Judaism (Acts 2:5, 41). On this reading, Peter was not condemning the Jewish people as a race; there was nothing crooked about being Jewish. He was warning about his own generation, which had rejected the Messiah and was heading toward the judgment Jesus had foretold. Those who believed were rescued, as Jesus promised the elect would be (Matthew 24:22). This is also a needed guard against antisemitism: the text blames a generation's response, not a people's birth.
Deuteronomy 32:5 uses similar words, "a perverse and crooked generation," of the wilderness generation.
Philippians 2:15 uses the same phrase for the world around the church in Philippi.

Those who read genea as "race" respond that the phrase describes unbelieving Israel as a group, not just one age. Most other interpreters, futurist or not, agree Acts 2:40 means Peter's contemporaries.
Does Hebrews 3:10, "I was angry with that generation," support the "race" meaning?
No. It speaks of one generation, the Israelites who wandered forty years in the wilderness.

Hebrews quotes Psalm 95: your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years; therefore I was angry with that generation (Hebrews 3:9-10). The generation in view is the one that left Egypt and died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29-35; 32:13). Their children entered the land. So the verse is about one span of people, not the whole race. On this reading, it also gives a helpful link. The wilderness generation lasted forty years. The time from Jesus' prophecy (about AD 30-33) to the fall of Jerusalem (AD 70) was roughly the same. The writer of Hebrews warns his readers not to repeat that generation's unbelief, because "today" was still open (Hebrews 3:13).
Numbers 32:13: God made them wander forty years until all that generation had died.
About forty years separate the crucifixion (AD 30 or 33) and the burning of the temple (AD 70).

Few interpreters use Hebrews 3:10 for the "race" view today. Futurists who reject AD 70 point out that "forty years" is a rough biblical figure and should not be pressed into a fixed rule for prophecy.
How do Bible translations render genea in Matthew 24:34?
Almost all major translations say "generation." Some list "race" only in a footnote as an alternative.

The King James Version, the American Standard Version (1901), the Revised Standard, the New English Bible, the New King James, the Jerusalem Bible, the New International Version and the New American Standard all read "generation" in Matthew 24:34. Some, such as the NIV and NASB, have a footnote offering "race" as an alternative. On this reading, the agreement of translators from many traditions is telling. If "race" were the plain meaning, one would expect at least some major translations to put it in the text. The translators judged that the context is about time, not ethnic survival.
KJV (1611): "This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled."
Young's Literal Translation (1862) also reads "this generation."

Supporters of "race" reply that translation choices do not settle the theology, since translators may follow tradition. They note the footnotes show the alternative was taken seriously by scholars, and that context and theology, not majority choice, must decide the meaning.
Did leading futurists accept the "race" reading of genea?
Not all. Hal Lindsey said the context is about time, not race, and called "race" a remote meaning of the word.

In a 1977 interview with Eternity magazine, Hal Lindsey was asked whether "this generation" might mean the race of people. He said no, because the context speaks of time, not race. He called "race" a very remote meaning of the word. Lindsey did not apply the generation to Jesus' hearers, though. He applied it to the generation that saw Israel reborn in 1948. On this reading, Lindsey's rejection of "race" is an important admission. Once genea means people living at one time, the question is only which time. The context of Matthew 24, addressed to the disciples, points to the first century.
Lindsey, Eternity, January 1977: he said he had debated the point with Earl Radmacher.
J. Dwight Pentecost, by contrast, called the "race" view the best explanation in Things to Come (1958).
